content.text:
**The Mom Test** is a customer-discovery technique from Rob Fitzpatrick’s book *The Mom Test*. The idea is: **ask questions so concrete and unbiased that even your mom couldn’t just politely lie and tell you your idea is great.**

The core principle: **don’t ask people whether your idea is good. Ask about their real past behavior, current problems, and what they’ve already tried.**

Bad questions:
- “Do you like my app idea?”
- “Would you use this?”
- “Would you pay $10/month for it?”
- “Do you think this is a problem?”

Better Mom Test questions:
- “How do you currently handle this?”
- “When was the last time this happened?”
- “What did you do about it?”
- “How much time or money does this cost you?”
- “What have you already tried?”
- “Who else is involved in solving this?”
- “What happens if you don’t solve it?”

The test helps you avoid false validation. People are often nice, optimistic, or hypothetical. They may say, “Yeah, I’d totally use that,” but that doesn’t mean they actually will.

A simple rule of thumb:

> **Talk about their life, not your idea.  
> Ask about specifics in the past, not opinions about the future.  
> Listen for problems, not compliments.**

Example:

Instead of saying:

> “I’m building an AI meal-planning app. Would you use it?”

Ask:

> “How do you decide what to cook during the week?”  
> “When was the last time meal planning was stressful?”  
> “What did you do?”  
> “Have you paid for any tools, cookbooks, apps, or services to help?”  

If they’ve never tried to solve the problem, never spent money, and don’t describe it as painful, that’s weak evidence. If they already use spreadsheets, pay for meal kits, complain about wasted groceries, or have hacked together a workaround, that’s stronger evidence.
